title: What goes into our post-tour follow-up

content.job: Standalone list email. Tell the full exchange from more tours and unanswered follow-up to the client's within-a-week practice and prospective texts. Connect the point to the complete LeadLock system with one reply invitation.
content.body:
She told me she pays attention to whether her venue is the first stop on a couple's tour list or the last one.

When she knows it's the last, she gets in touch within a week. She asks, directly and politely, whether they've picked their venue or haven't decided yet. It's a question that fits a couple who has finished looking.

A couple fresh off their first tour is in a different place. They're still comparing, and they may not be ready to answer that.

**Before we shape follow-up for a venue, we want to know how far along each couple is in choosing.**

She already had automated follow-up emails in place, and she was reaching out personally on top of them. She raised the idea of adding texts after the tour, and I told her we could work those in.

Here's why her distinction matters to us. You're already generating inquiries, hosting tours and talking with couples yourself. The support around that work should build on what you learn during the visit, so a couple who's still comparing and a couple who's close to deciding each hear something that fits where they are.

LeadLock is the platform where we build your email and text follow-up. Inside it, we set up The Foolproof Follow-Up Advantage, our email-and-text follow-up system, around your own conversations. You run the platform, and the personal contact couples get from you stays yours.
content.ending:
If you'd like follow-up support shaped around what you learn on your tours, simply reply to this email and let's talk about your business.

Talk soon,
Whitney

content.title: First tour or last tour
content.script:
I had a call with one of our venue clients recently, and she was booking more tours, but more of those couples were going quiet afterwards.

So I asked her a question. When couples leave a tour, do they still have other venues to see, or are they ready to move forward?

And she explained that she gauges one thing: is her venue their first tour, or their last?

When she knows it's their last, she reaches out within a week and asks, really politely, if they've made their choice or they're still undecided.

I thought that was such a smart distinction.

Because a couple who's just started touring is still comparing, right? They're not necessarily ready for that question yet.

Now, she already had automated emails going out, and she was following up personally on top of that. She'd been thinking about texting couples after the tour, too, and I told her we could add that.

So when we shape follow-up after a tour, the fact that a couple visited is only part of the picture. We want to know what they're ready to do next, so every email and text supports the conversation you're already having with them.

caption.body:
Couples found you, inquired and came out to see the venue in person. You walked them through it and helped them picture the day. Then some of them stop answering, and you're left wondering whether they're still deciding or have moved on.

I talked about this with one of our venue clients recently. Her tours were up, and so was the number of couples going quiet. I asked whether those couples walked out with more visits planned or ready to take the next step.

She explained that she gauges where her venue falls in a couple's search. If it's their final visit, she follows up within a week and asks, kindly and plainly, whether they've made a decision. Someone at the start of their search isn't necessarily ready for that.

She already had automated emails working next to her own personal outreach, and when she raised adding post-tour texts, I said we could add those.

What you learn on a tour tells us what the next message should make room for. The emails and texts support the contact you're already having with couples, at the point in the search they've actually reached.
caption.hook: When more couples tour your venue and more of them go quiet, it's worth asking where they were in their search.

content.takeaway: A couple who toured my venue isn't automatically ready to decide, and my follow-up should fit where they are in their search.

caption.body:
You already put care into helping couples picture their wedding at your venue. After the visit, you want to keep that conversation moving without assuming everyone has finished looking.

A venue client described more tour bookings alongside more couples who weren't responding. I asked whether they left with other venues to visit or were ready to move forward.

She explained that she gauges where her venue falls in their tour list. If it's their final visit, she politely asks within a week whether they've chosen a venue or are still undecided. Someone at the beginning of that list is still comparing options.

She had automated emails and was also reaching out personally. When she raised including post-tour texts, I agreed that we could incorporate them.

Your conversations on the tour can tell us what the next message needs to make room for, while email and text support the contact you continue to have with the couple.

I had a call with one of our venue clients recently, and she was booking more tours, but more of those couples were going quiet afterwards.

So I asked her a question. When couples leave a tour, do they still have other venues to see, or are they ready to move forward?

And she explained that she gauges one thing: is her venue their first tour, or their last?

When she knows it's their last, she reaches out within a week and asks, really politely, if they've made their choice or they're still undecided.

I thought that was such a smart distinction.

Because a couple who's just started touring is still comparing, right? They're not necessarily ready for that question yet.

Now, she already had automated emails going out, and she was following up personally on top of that. She'd been thinking about texting couples after the tour, too, and I told her we could add that.

So when we shape follow-up after a tour, the fact that a couple visited is only part of the picture. We want to know what they're ready to do next, so every email and text supports the conversation you're already having with them.

content.title: The week after a final tour
content.script:
How soon should you follow up after a couple's last venue tour?

One of our venue clients walked me through how she handles this, and I really liked her reasoning.

When she knows her venue was the final stop on a couple's list, she checks in within a week. She asks them, nicely and properly, whether they've gone with a different venue or they're still undecided.

She also told me that at her venue, when hers is the last tour, couples usually know within the next few days, more often than not.

She also mentioned that follow-up for those last-tour couples might need to be customized a little, because they're in a different spot than a couple who's just starting to look.

That's the kind of thing we listen for when we help shape a venue's follow-up. How quickly her couples decide is something she learned from her own tours, and it tells us a lot about when a message should go out and what it should ask.

caption.body:
After a great final tour, the next message still has to go out, and it's hard to know when it should arrive or what it should ask. Wait too long and you're guessing. Ask too soon and it can feel like pressure on a couple who isn't done looking.

One of our venue clients has a clear habit here. When she knows her venue closed out a couple's search, she gets in touch inside of a week with one direct, courteous question about whether they've decided.

She also shared something from her own tours: at her venue, when hers is a couple's last stop, they usually know within the next few days, more often than not.

She also pointed out that couples on their last tour may need follow-up that's a little more customized than couples who are just starting out.

That's the kind of detail we want guiding follow-up for a venue: the pace her couples actually decide at, learned firsthand, rather than one schedule for every couple who walks through the door.

caption.body:
Maybe you've built your own rhythm after tours. Automated emails go out, and you follow up yourself with the couples you connected with. Then you notice a gap and wonder whether you need something more.

That's where one of our venue clients was. She had an automatic follow-up sequence running, and she was reaching out personally on top of it, partly because she didn't have texts set up for after the tour. She wondered whether she should do something about that, and I told her we could incorporate it.

The texts are still an idea we agreed on. What matters to us is what was already in place: automated emails and her own personal follow-up, with the texts as something she raised herself.

For her, any texts we add would sit beside the emails and the personal follow-up she's already doing, not in place of them.

before_publishing.text:
A line a person wrote for the earlier Reel 3 was not carried into its new premise: More tours are a good sign. But a tour on your calendar doesn't tell you whether the couple is on their first visit or their last, and unanswered follow-up looks the same either way.

This came up with one of our venue clients. I asked whether couples left planning other visits or ready to move forward. Her answer was that she watches whether her venue opened their search or closed it.

When she knows they've finished touring, she reaches out within a week and politely asks if they've landed on a venue or are still undecided. A couple who has only begun visiting is still comparing what they've seen.

She already paired automated emails with her personal contact, and she asked about texting couples after the tour as well. I said we could add that.

That's the kind of detail we want shaping the emails and texts around your conversations, so each couple hears from you in a way that suits how far their search has come.
